newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Albright warns Croats, Serbs on war crimes.
newsitem.headline: Albright warns Croats, Serbs on war crimes.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright warned on Wednesday that there is "no statute of limitations on war crimes" and vowed that Serbia, Croatia and Bosnian Serbs would face financial and other penalties until those accused of atrocities were brought to justice.

In a lightning visit to the war crimes tribunal at the Hague that she helped establish as U.N. ambassdor, Albright expressed confidence that a renewed U.S. effort to pressure Zagreb, Belgrade and Pale to turn over indicted war criminals for trial would be successful.

She said that when she visits Serbia and Croatia at the weekend she would carry "a new and tougher message to (Croatian President Franjo) Tudjman and (Serbian President Slobodan) Milosevic, saying basically their lack of cooperation in this area is a roadblock to our cooperation with them and their ability to really be full members of the international community."

Four years since it was set up by the U.N. Security Council, the Hague tribunal has indicted 75 suspected war criminals, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic, who remain at large like the majority of other suspects.

Only nine have been arrested and sent to The Hague, including Bosnian Croat prison camp commander Zlatko Aleksovski. Croatia handed him over last month only after U.S. threats to block major loans to the country.
Albright insisted that "pressure is building on the leaders within those countries to turn the war criminals over."

She refused to say if there were any plans to create a special military unit to cature war criminals. She said she would discuss "options" with ministers of Russia, France, Britain and Germany in Sintra, Portugal on Friday.

U.S. officials said she would tell Milosevic "there is not a chance" Washington would support Serbian access to international lending or succeeding to the U.N. seat of Yugoslavia without more cooperation.
Similarly, Croatia will be opposed for international loans and menbership in NATO's partnership for peace organixation and other western institutions, officials said.

Although it lasted less than 30 minutes, Albright's meeting with chief war crimes tribunal prosecutor Louise Arbour was meant to focus a spotlight on the prosecution of Bosnian war criminals, a troubled process that is viewed by experts as a major threat to the 1995 Dayton peace agreement.
She stopped at the tribunal on the fringes of a U.S.- European Union summit at the Hague.

A senior official who last week outlined details of a new U.S. campaign to re-invigorate the flagging Bosnia peace process said "bringing war criminals to justice" is now the administration's top priority.

But Washington has failed to make public any specific new strategy to achieve that goal, a feature of the 1995 U.S.- brokered Dayton accords that experts say is essential to any hope of a lasting peace in Bosnia.

Ambassador Robert Gelbard, the new U,S. Bosnia coordinator, failed on Monday in the latest attempt to persuade Milosevic to comply with the Dayton peace accords and deliver indicted suspects to justice.
Diplomats have predicted Milosevic would refuse to hand over war crimes suspects before Serbian elections due by the end of the year.
Belgrade refuses to deliver three senior Yugoslav army officers indicted in connection with atrocities in the Croatian town of Vukovar during the six-month Croatian-Serb war in 1991.

Washington says it does not know the whereabouts of all the indicted suspects. But a senior U.S. official insisted "we're looking at every possible way to bring war criminals to justice" including a proposal for a special military unit to track down suspects for delivery to the Hague.

The NATO-led stabilisation force in Bosnia, which U.S. troops dominate, is not charged with ferreting out war criminals, although political leaders have insisted the troops would arrest suspects if they encoutered them in the normal course of business.
But so far they have not done so, fuelling suspicions that the Pentagon, which has resisted involvement with the war crime issue, had a deliberately avoided suspects.

To get around this problem, U.S. officials have explored creating a special military unit to track down indicted suspects. There has been some opposition from Europe but U.S. officials say this is not universal and the idea remains alive.

Theodor Meron, who helped the tribunal prosecute Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic for war crimes in 1995, wrote in a recent Foreign Affairs magazine that "the international community has given the tribunal strong rhetorical support but little aid in enforcement."

He called this a "disgrace" and said suspects could have been captured by the NATO-led forces "without serious casualties, especially with the help from the intelligence community. The risk was worth taking."
